title: Designing access separation between business units

opening.headline: When sharing the same knowledge base while needing to separate access across business units, you learn how to determine the separation level by balancing risk and operational costs.
body: Company policies and product introductions are common knowledge shared across all business divisions. Conversely, pricing and customer data for each business division should be accessible only to that specific division. While common knowledge should be managed once, proprietary data must not leak out.

In this class, we sequentially examine three approaches to implementation of separation: tenant separation, index separation, and filter-based separation. We compare these approaches based on three criteria: leakage risk, operational cost, and reuse of common knowledge. The stronger the separation, the higher the cost and operational burden becomes; conversely, weaker separation increases leakage risk. Finally, we illustrate a case where the structure combining shared knowledge and business-unit-specific knowledge is designed according to sensitivity levels.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Index separation, filtering, and tenant separation can be compared based on leak risks and operational costs.
It is possible to assess whether the balance between separation level and operational costs is appropriate.

screens.title: Same knowledge base, different scope of approach
screens.lead: First, read about the scenario where general knowledge and specialized knowledge are placed on a common foundation. Consider what issues arise when separation is strongly enforced versus when it is weakly enforced.

visual.alt: This is a diagram that separates the level of separation between common knowledge, accessible to all business units, and business-unit-specific knowledge, readable only by the respective business unit.

paragraphs: Common knowledge within an organization includes company policies and product introductions. Since all business divisions must read and base their decisions on the same content, this information should be managed only once. In contrast, pricing lists and customer data specific to each business division are dedicated knowledge that should be accessible only to the respective division.

To use these two types of knowledge within a single knowledge base, a separation level must be defined. A weak separation allows common knowledge to be easily reused, but increases the risk of specialized knowledge leaking if one filter fails. A strong separation reduces leakage risks but increases synchronization with environment and policies, raising operational costs and making it harder to share common knowledge.
Therefore, higher separation is not always better. Determining a separation level involves making a judgment about balancing risks and costs.
The question to be answered in this class is this: How is the separation level determined?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: It may seem safe to separate all materials as strongly as possible. However, consider the issues that would arise if even common knowledge had to be replicated across each business unit.

screens.outro: Let me first recall my experience handling a separation request.

screens.title: Recall an experience dealing with a requirement for data access separation
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Who demanded separation? Was it regulation, customers, or internal policy?
items.answer: The required strength for separation depends on the entity making the request. Requirements arising from regulations or customer contracts often call for structural separation, while requirements from internal policies may only require separation at the filter level. Confirming the source of the requirement is the starting point for determining the separation level.

You might have implemented one of the following approaches: separating the environment, splitting indexes, or applying conditions on queries, possibly combining them. In this course, these three methods are referred to as tenant separation, index separation, and filter-based separation, and are compared accordingly.

items.prompt: Who bears the cost of this separation?
items.answer: Separate costs often accumulate silently. As the environment grows, so do accounts, configurations, and policies, and their management falls to the operations team. It becomes possible to determine who bears the cost, enabling better decisions about risk and expense allocation.

screens.outro: Let's start by examining the strongest separation: tenant separation.

screens.title: Tenant Isolation: Strongest Isolation

terms.tip: Each business unit is given an independent environment to ensure that data, configurations, and permissions are not structurally mixed. While this approach provides the highest level of separation, it also results in the highest operational costs.

This is the unit responsible for managing members, seats, feature access, and analytics in ChatGPT Enterprise. When workspaces are divided by business unit, the management scope is also divided accordingly.

This means that mixing is impossible because the environment itself is different, not due to filter settings. Even if there is a configuration error, it will not affect data from other environments.

If there are two environments, you end up managing the same policies and accounts twice. The more environments there are, the more repeatedly tasks such as policy changes and user account cleanups occur.

screens.outro: Let us now continue examining index partitioning within a single environment.

screens.title: Index separation: divide the store by business unit
screens.lead: When an item is selected, the structure and advantages, as well as the costs, of index separation are displayed. Note that index separation is one step lighter than tenant separation.

visual.alt: A structure where queries are divided between departmental data stores and a shared store.

items.title: Structure: Divides the store and limits the query target
items.body: Gemini Enterprise creates a separate data store for each entity within a data source. For example, with Jira, stores are created for entities such as issues, attachments, and comments. By partitioning stores by business unit within this structure, user queries can be directed only to the allowed stores. The query receiver verifies the user's affiliation and then determines the appropriate set of target stores.

items.title: Advantage: Filter errors do not immediately become leaks
items.body: Within a single store, incorrectly applying a filter will not grant access to documents from other business units since those documents do not exist in that store. This is a key difference from filter-based separation, where a single filter error directly leads to a leak. Instead, this approach proactively blocks potential errors arising from human misconfiguration through structural safeguards.

items.title: Cost: Synchronization with shared documents
items.body: Common documents must either be replicated per business unit or require separate queries to a dedicated shared store. Replication introduces inconsistencies and synchronization overhead, while querying a dedicated shared store leads to complex query and result merging. Additionally, synchronization intervals must be managed for each store, increasing operational burden as the number of stores grows.

items.title: Design considerations: storage region
items.body: When collecting data, you must select the region where the data will be stored, such as global, United States, or EU. If each business unit has different regulatory requirements or contracts that necessitate different storage locations, then a design that divides the storage can also satisfy these requirements.

screens.outro: We will continue with a discussion on filter-based separation, the final method, and a comparison of the three approaches.

screens.title: Filter-based separation and three-method comparison
screens.lead: The following table compares three separation approaches based on three criteria: leak risk, operational cost, and shared knowledge reuse. As one moves from top to bottom, separation weakens and operations become lighter.

data.notes: In filter-based separation, the backend of the RAG reference architecture constructs search filters during the pre-processing stage prior to search. This approach carries risks because the speed at which authorization changes are reflected in the index depends on synchronization. There is no definitive answer as to which method is correct; instead, approaches are typically combined based on the sensitivity of the knowledge involved. When reading the table, one should note that the three criteria are not independent of each other. Strengthening separation to reduce leakage risks increases operational costs and hampers reuse of common knowledge, resulting in a correlated effect. Therefore, selecting a method based on only one criterion will lead to problems when evaluated against other criteria. Additionally, when choosing filter-based separation, it is essential to consolidate filters into a single location and establish a procedure to verify that access metadata is not lost when new documents are added, in order to reduce risks.

screens.outro: Now, I will illustrate a design that combines all three approaches as an example.

screens.title: Explanation: Structure combining common and dedicated knowledge (1) Classification
screens.lead: The instructor follows the process of classifying a structure that combines common knowledge and specialized knowledge by sensitivity level. Selecting the right arrow proceeds to the next step. Note that knowledge is divided first, and the method is determined later.

visual.alt: A diagram showing knowledge divided into common, business unit-specific, and regulatory categories, each deployed using a different separation approach.
labels: Strong separation at the tenant or standalone store level

steps.title: Step 1: Divide knowledge by sensitivity level
steps.body: First, divide knowledge into three categories. Common knowledge accessible to all business units, business-specific knowledge readable only by a particular business unit, and regulatory or contractual knowledge that must be strictly separated due to compliance requirements. We perform classification before determining the approach because applying the same level of protection to all knowledge would result in excessive costs or unmitigated risks.

steps.title: Step 2: Designate regulatory candidates as strong separation candidates.
steps.body: Regulated knowledge is best considered at the tenant isolation or separate store level with strong separation. In such cases, even a single filter error can be difficult to handle. It is more reasonable to choose a structurally decoupled approach, even if operational costs are high, since such knowledge is not voluminous and thus imposes limited cost burden.

steps.title: Step 3: The business unit's dedicated instance is designated as a candidate for index separation.
steps.body: Department-specific knowledge is considered as an index partitioning approach by separating data stores per department. It allows for isolated environments without requiring full tenant separation, avoiding data leakage from filter errors. It represents a balanced middle ground between risk and cost.

steps.title: Step 4: Keep the common one as read-only in a single shared index.
steps.body: Common knowledge is stored in a single shared index and granted read-only access to all business units. Since it requires only one management effort, operations are lightweight and consistency is guaranteed. While it may seem safer to replicate common knowledge across each business unit, replication introduces synchronization overhead and content inconsistencies.

screens.outro: The classification is complete; now let's move on to the second section, determining the query flow and balance.

screens.title: Explanation: Structure combining common and dedicated knowledge (2) Design and balance
screens.lead: This is the second part of the explanation. We will follow the process of designing how queries flow over the classified structure and determine the separation level.

steps.title: Step 5: When making a query, specify the allowed store based on the user's affiliation.
steps.body: When a query arrives, first verify the user's affiliation and determine the set of stores they are allowed to access. In the RAG reference architecture, the unified backend performs preprocessing before search, so incorporating this step into the backend's preprocessing ensures that the same criteria are applied regardless of whether the frontend or backend handles it. Queries are not sent to unauthorized stores.

steps.title: Step 6: Query both the shared store and the business unit store together.
steps.body: The allowed store set includes both shared stores and stores belonging to user-owned business units. After querying both locations, the results are merged to form the response. If a business unit is under regulatory scope, the corresponding strong separation store is also included using the same method. The key point is that merging occurs only within the allowed set.

steps.title: Step 7: Install a filter on the shared side as well to provide dual protection.
steps.body: Just because a shared store is set to read-only does not mean filters are unnecessary. By placing access conditions on the shared side to prevent business-unit-specific documents from being incorrectly indexed, if one side's configuration goes wrong, the other side can block it. This creates a dual defense by combining structural separation with filtering.

steps.title: Step 8: Determine the separation level by comparing operational costs and risk reduction.
steps.body: Finally, operational costs associated with the number of stores and synchronization frequency are compared against the risk reduction benefits. While splitting business units into more stores reduces risk, it also increases synchronization and management costs. The optimal level of segmentation is determined by evaluating whether the costs are acceptable and whether the reduced risk is actually meaningful. Documenting the rationale behind this decision enables future structural changes to reuse this analysis.

screens.outro: We will consolidate and summarize the conclusion of the case on a single screen.

screens.title: Separation level is an exchange between risk and cost.
screens.lead: We summarize the content reviewed so far as the criteria for evaluating our architecture's separation level.

paragraphs: Access segregation is divided into three types: tenant segregation, index segregation, and filter-based segregation. As segregation progresses from tenant to index to filter, segregation becomes less strict and operations become lighter. The method with the lowest leakage risk also has the highest operational cost, while the method with the lightest operations carries the highest leakage risk. Risk and cost are inversely related to each other.

Therefore, it is common practice to distribute knowledge based on sensitivity levels and mix access methods accordingly, rather than applying a single approach across the entire system. Regulatory data is separated with strong isolation, business unit-specific data uses index isolation, and shared data is kept in a single, read-only public index. Fully isolating all knowledge leads to excessive operational overhead, while isolating only through filters makes it impossible for regulatory data to handle filter errors.

At the query stage, the system defines a permitted storage set based on the user's affiliation and performs only queries and merges within that set. A filter is also applied on the public side, combining structural separation with filtering to provide dual-layer protection. This design ensures that errors in one device do not immediately result in data leakage.

When assessing the balance of separation levels, you only need to ask three questions: What level of damage would result if this knowledge were to leak? Is the operational cost to prevent that damage acceptable to bear? Does this knowledge impose any barriers to reusing common knowledge? If the answers to these three questions differ depending on the category of knowledge, then the separation level should also vary by category.

Finally, when documenting separation of concerns, the following items should be included: the categories of knowledge and their sensitivity levels, a balanced approach to separation by category along with the rationale behind it, rules defining which storage systems are allowed during queries, filters placed on the shared side, synchronization intervals, and a comparison of operational costs versus risk reduction. With this document in place, when business units expand or regulations change and require a reevaluation of the separation level, decisions can be made by simply reflecting the changed conditions without having to restart the entire discussion. Separation of concerns is not a one-time task that is completed and finished—it is an ongoing process that must be reviewed whenever risks or costs change.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The separation level is an exchange between risk and cost. Divide knowledge by sensitivity levels, combining strong and loose separation, and add filters on the shared side for dual-layer defense.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: What kind of isolation is needed to ensure that one store's incorrect filtering does not affect documents from other business units?
options: Queries are directed only to the data store specific to each business unit.
When accessing a index, attach group metadata and query with conditions
Filters the document one more time just before providing the response
Maintain a single shared index in read-only mode, without distinguishing by business unit.
checks.explain: Index segregation is a structural separation that ensures queries do not reach other business unit stores even if filter errors occur. Instead, it incurs costs associated with common document replication, shared store queries, and store-specific synchronization.

wrong.1: Filter-based means one missing filter equals one leak.
wrong.2: The response-before filter can only compensate for errors from the previous stage after the fact.
wrong.3: A single index is for common knowledge and is not a means to separate dedicated data.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. By dividing the store, filter errors will not immediately become leaks.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. Recall what it means to block based on structure, rather than relying on filters.

glossary.def: This is the strongest separation method, providing an independent environment for each business unit.
This approach divides the data store (index) by business unit to limit the scope of queries.
This is a method where metadata is attached to a single index and conditions are applied during querying to isolate results.
The management burden resulting from an increasing number of environments, stores, synchronization, and policies.

misconceptions.myth: The more frequent the partitioning, the better.
misconceptions.fact: The higher the separation, the higher the operational costs become and the more difficult it is to reuse shared knowledge. A level appropriate to the sensitivity of the knowledge is the right level.
A missing filter is simply a leak. Sensitive knowledge must be reinforced with structural separation.

misconceptions.myth: Shared knowledge is safer when duplicated across business units.
misconceptions.fact: Replication incurs synchronization overhead and content inconsistency. It is better to keep a single shared index in read-only mode.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The separation level is an exchange between risk and cost.
Tenant, index, and filter separation weakens and operations become lighter.
Divide knowledge by sensitivity level and combine strong separation with light separation.
A filter is also provided on the common side for dual protection.
